narrative:
The 2017 Houston Astros arrived with championship expectations, and from the very first week they made clear they intended to meet them. George Springer set the tone on April 5th with a three-run home run that swung the win probability by more than 80 percent, an early signal that this was a team built for big moments. They raced through April at 16-9 and then absolutely demolished May, posting a stunning 22-7 record that announced them as the class of the American League. Grand slams from Marwin Gonzalez and Yuli Gurriel punctuated a month of relentless offensive production, and the lineup — led by Jose Altuve, Carlos Correa, and a cast of versatile contributors — lived up to every bit of its 896-run potential.

June and July brought a slight cooling, with the team going a combined 31-20 over those two months. Ken Giles showed early signs of unreliability in the closer's role, surrendering key home runs and doubles at the worst moments, yet the offense kept bailing the club out. Marwin Gonzalez continued his remarkable super-utility season with a go-ahead three-run blast in late July, and the rotation remained sturdy enough to keep the team in the AL West driver's seat. These months were a reminder that even the best teams play through turbulence — the Astros were winning ugly at times, but they were winning.

August was the one true rough patch of the season, a 11-17 month that raised genuine questions. Harvey, Irma, and Maria battered the Gulf Coast that month, and amid the devastation the Astros played tight, fractured baseball. Tyler Clippard gave up a back-breaking three-run homer to Andrelton Simmons. Giles kept struggling. Yet even inside the struggle, flashes of resilience appeared — Alex Bregman's clutch triple, Brian McCann's improbable game-turning three-run triple, and the lineup grinding out wins when the bullpen faltered. September answered every doubt, as the Astros roared back at 20-8, locking up the AL West and heading into October as one of the most feared teams in baseball.

The postseason was a showcase for Houston's heart. They dispatched the Red Sox in the Division Series and then toppled the New York Yankees in a seven-game ALCS. The World Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers provided the most dramatic baseball of the decade, with the Astros weathering Giles's continued late-game meltdowns and Dodger comebacks through seven breathless games. Marwin Gonzalez's solo homer in Game 2 sparked a comeback, Altuve hit bombs in the biggest moments, and Alex Bregman's walk-off single in Game 5 — one of the greatest World Series games ever played — turned the series. When the final out was recorded, Houston had its first World Series championship, a title that meant everything to a city still healing from Hurricane Harvey.

chapters.title: Fast Start, High Expectations
chapters.description: The Astros burst out of the gate in April with dominant performances, led by George Springer's massive opening statement and a roster that looked ready to contend from day one.

chapters.title: Best Team in Baseball
chapters.description: A blistering May — 22 wins in 29 games — cemented Houston's status as the AL's elite, fueled by grand slams, clutch hits, and an offense that simply refused to stop scoring.

chapters.title: Winning Through the Cracks
chapters.description: June and July saw the Astros navigate bullpen inconsistency and a few agonizing losses, yet continued to win games on the back of timely hitting and a resilient core lineup.

chapters.title: Harvey's Shadow and a September Surge
chapters.description: An 11-17 August — played against the backdrop of Hurricane Harvey's devastation — tested the team's character, before a fiery 20-8 September silenced every doubt and secured the division.

chapters.title: October Glory
chapters.description: Through a grueling seven-game World Series against the Dodgers, with Giles faltering and the Astros repeatedly staring down elimination, Houston's deepest stars — Altuve, Bregman, Gonzalez — delivered a championship for a city that needed it most.
